We started raising interest rates at the end of 2021 to help control inflation. Since then, it has fallen a lot and the pressures that caused price rises had eased. As a result, we were able to start reducing interest rates in August 2024 from 5.25% down to 3.75% in December 2025.
However, this was before war broke out in Iran and the Middle East. This has disrupted the transportation and supply of oil and gas and pushed up energy prices. Inflation reached 3.1% in August 2026.
Monetary policy cannot affect global energy prices; our job is to make sure that higher inflation does not persist and have long-lasting effects on the economy.
We are monitoring the situation closely and will do what is necessary to make sure that inflation stays on track to meet the 2% target in the medium term.
We make our decision on interest rates every six weeks or so. Each time, we look at the state of the economy and recent global developments, and what we expect for the coming months. The factors we consider include:
We will announce our next decision on Thursday 5 November 2026. You can see our full list of upcoming dates along with links to our more detailed reports.
Interest rates influence how much people spend, and that changes how shops and other businesses set their prices.
Higher interest rates lead to higher charges on many mortgages and loans, meaning people must spend more on them and less on other things.
It also means savers get a bigger return (ie they make more money by not spending) and potential borrowers find it is more expensive to take out a loan. These things make it less attractive for people and companies to spend money.
When people spend less, businesses are less willing or able to raise their prices. When prices do not go up so quickly, inflation falls.
Lower interest rates can have the reverse effect. If payments on mortgages and loans go down, people will have more money to spend on other things. Savers will get a smaller return and, therefore, may feel less motivated to put their money away. It will be also cheaper for potential borrowers to take out a loan – and use that money to make big purchases.
All of these factors encourage spending. When people spend more, this means demand is high. And when demand is high, businesses often raise their prices, pushing up inflation.
The Bank of England sets Bank Rate. It is also sometimes known simply as 'the interest rate'.
It is the rate of interest we pay to commercial banks, building societies and financial institutions that hold money with us. It is also the rate we charge on loans we may make to them.
Bank Rate, therefore, affects the level of all other interest rates in the UK. When we raise it, banks will usually increase how much they charge their customers on loans (to cover the increased cost) and the interest they offer on savings. This tends to discourage businesses from taking out loans to fund investment and encourages people to save rather than spend.
Experience tells us that when overall spending is lower, prices stop rising so quickly and inflation slows down.
The reverse happens when we reduce Bank Rate. Banks cut the rates they offer on loans and savings. That gives people freedom to spend more, which they tend to do.
Bank Rate was almost zero (0.1%) at the beginning of December 2021. It is 3.75% now.
In the years between 1975 and 2007, Bank Rate was 3.5% at its lowest point and 17% at its highest. We cut it to 0.5% during the global financial crisis in 2008 and 2009. We kept it low after that to support the economy.
People have told us directly that they are finding higher mortgage and loan payments very difficult. They also ask if higher interest rates are the best option we have.
The answer is yes. The Government sets us a target of getting inflation to 2% – and interest rates are the best tool we have to slow down price rises.
We know that interest rates are an effective tool for managing inflation because they have been used successfully across many countries and circumstances. They are effective in influencing the amount of spending in the economy and, therefore, inflation.
Inflation has come down a long way since its peak almost four years ago – the events that led to price rises settled down and raising interest rates had the desired effect.
But it is very difficult to predict how the economy will evolve. We said another global shock could change the situation significantly and that has proved to be true as the war in the Middle East goes on. It has already affected energy prices and means inflation is still above the 2% target.
It was at 3.3% in March 2026 but went down to 2.8% in April. This was largely due to the reduction in the Government's energy price cap for April to June. It stayed at that level for May, due to slowing food price rises. Then in June it went down to 2.6% after the temporary ceasefire in the Middle East led to a drop in petrol and diesel prices. Summer clothing discounts and falling food prices also contributed to this.
It then rose to 2.9% in July, then 3.1% in August. These increases were again largely due to energy costs. So far, there is little evidence of significant knock-on effects on businesses' price and wage setting. But the scale of the impact on inflation will depend on how long the war (and its effect on the global energy supply) lasts.
The war has disrupted the production and transportation of goods, including oil and gas. It has also shut down important facilities used to produce them.
The number of ships moving through the Strait of Hormuz, off Iran – a route through which about a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas passes – has fallen by a large amount.
When these resources cannot reach their destination, supply goes down but demand stays the same. And, put simply, when there's not much of something but lots of people want it, the price goes up.
The temporary ceasefire caused energy prices to fall back from the initial spike in early 2026. But peace negotiations broke down and the conflict resumed, so energy prices have been very volatile and are hard to predict.
Higher oil and gas prices feed into inflation in the UK because we rely on energy to heat our homes and fuel our cars, as well as to produce most of the goods and services we pay or charge for. Energy purchases made up about 8% of household spending in 2024 on average.
Of course, these higher prices lead to higher gas and fuel bills – but they also lead to higher electricity bills. Power stations that run on gas often set the price of electricity; when gas becomes more expensive, those plants raise the price of the electricity they generate to cover the cost.
So, when global energy markets spike, the costs rise for households and businesses in our country, and this can then have a knock-on effect. If firms' bills go up, they may need to raise the prices of the goods and services that they sell to cover the cost. And workers may ask for higher wages as their bills also rise. This would all push up inflation.
Having said that, there isn’t very high demand for workers right now, ie there are more people looking for work than there are jobs available. So, employers may feel less pressure to increase salaries.
Interest rates charged by high street banks to households and businesses are also higher than before the war. These, combined with slow wage growth, could make people more cautious about spending, counteracting the effects of higher energy prices and keeping inflation from going up too much. But it depends on how long energy prices stay raised.
We also expect ‘real incomes’ to fall as the prices of non-energy products rise. This means that the money households have coming in may stay the same, but it will buy less than it used to.
The first was the coronavirus pandemic. There was a large shortage of products and services, then as lockdowns eased there was suddenly huge demand for them and inflation rose. As we've already established, when there's not much of something but lots of people want it, the price goes up.
We knew that wouldn't last long. But then came Russia's invasion of Ukraine, which had a large impact on energy and food prices.
For example, the war caused the supply of gas from Russia to drop significantly and gas prices rose as a result. Higher energy costs make it more expensive for businesses to produce other goods and services – so they raised their prices as well.
The third was a shortage of workers available in the UK. Thousands dropped out of the workforce after the pandemic, which raised the cost of hiring. So, some businesses put up their prices to cover those costs.
